themes: Capex Intensity and Balance Sheet Strength
key_points: Cell-integrated manufacturers earn ~31% EBITDA margins vs 7.7-17.6% for module-only peers, a 23+ percentage point gap
Domestic cell capacity shortage (57.1GW cells vs 204.9GW modules) supports DCR premiums of Rs8.9/Wp (~69%) over non-DCR
124GW cell capacity supply wave expected by FY27E against 60GW demand will reset DCR premiums downward in FY28
US AD/CVD duties of 249.13% effective Oct-2026 close Indian export market; Waaree wrote off 3GW+ orders
Cell line utilization at 81-99% vs module lines at 44-68% reflects structural imbalance favoring integrated players

DCR spreads of USD7-8 cents/Wp vs non-DCR USD1-2 cents/Wp create unsustainable economics for non-integrated peers
150GW+ RE construction pipeline supports volumes through FY28, but new award flow weakness threatens FY29-30 demand

DCR premium reset as 124GW cell capacity commissioned against 60GW demand by FY27E

PM Surya Ghar Phase-II and KUSUM expansion driving retail and agricultural DCR demand

reports.summary: India's solar manufacturing sector is shifting from module-centric capacity additions to cell-integrated value chains, with integration now defining profitability. Cell-integrated players earn 31% EBITDA margins versus 7.7% for module-only manufacturers, driven by severe domestic cell scarcity (57GW cells vs 205GW modules) and 70% DCR premiums. However, a 124GW cell capacity wave arriving in FY27-28 against 60GW demand will compress these spreads by FY28, making execution, balance-sheet strength and captive cell ownership critical differentiators. Premier Energies is the top pick for superior cell integration, while module-only players and leveraged peers face margin compression and execution risk.
reports.connection_narrative: India's solar manufacturing sector is experiencing a structural inflection from volume-driven module capacity to integration-led profitability, driven by domestic content requirements under ALMM framework and the closure of the US export market following 249% AD/CVD duties in October 2026. This policy shift, combined with the government's massive push for renewable energy to meet 500GW non-fossil targets by 2030, is creating two parallel dynamics: first, a severe domestic cell supply shortage where 57GW of ALMM-approved cell capacity must serve 205GW of module-making capability, generating extraordinary DCR premiums of 70% and EBITDA spreads of USD7-8 cents per watt for integrated players; and second, a pending supply wave of 124GW new cell capacity arriving in FY27-28 that will invert these economics by FY28. The demand side remains robust with 44.6GW added in FY26 and rooftop PM Surya Ghar systems accelerating (2.4 million in H1FY27), but weak utility-scale award flow and 8,100GWh of grid curtailment signal emerging transmission constraints. Within this landscape, Premier Energies stands out with 10.6GW of TOPCon cell capacity reaching commercial readiness in December 2026 and 70% utilization by March 2027, combined with 11.1GW module integration and internally-funded capex from operating cash flow, positioning it to capture both the current cell-scarcity premiums and maintain margin resilience as supplies normalize. Waaree, despite maintaining net cash of Rs32.2 billion and announcing 15GW cell capacity by FY27E, faces execution risks on its ambitious Rs300 billion capex program where only 35% is deployed and 37% remains in planning; its exposure to US manufacturing through the 4.8GW Texas facility mitigates some export closure impact but creates execution and ramp-up risks. In stark contrast, module-only players including Vikram Solar, Saatvik Green, and Insolation Energy operate under structural margin compression where non-DCR module spreads of only USD1-2 cents per watt force them into immediate cell-purchase economics at USD14-14.5 cents per watt to earn USD1 cent per watt on non-DCR utility modules, making each month of ALMM List-II approval delay catastrophic; Saatvik's debt-to-equity already at 1.37x with large 5.6GW capex underway signals refinancing risk if utilization delays extend. The critical catalyst to monitor is the actual commissioning timeline of Waaree's first 5GW cell line by Q3FY27 and Premier's ramp to 70% utilization by March 2027, as delays would extend the DCR premium window but delays of more than two quarters would force module-only players into insolvency. The paramount risk is Chinese equipment controls on wafer-making technology, the next capex frontier required by ALMM List-III in June 2028, which could either block indigenous wafer ambitions or force technology compromises that undermine the integration thesis entirely.
